court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Fourth Department
holding_summary: A cotenant could be charged only for the rental value of portions he occupied adversely, rather than for the entire property. Other cotenants likewise could be charged for portions they occupied or rents they collected, making an accounting appropriate.

quotes.text: The dwelling house was continuously occupied by the same tenant until the time of the trial, and the rent fqr it was collected either by Jay Loomis or Rachael Loomis; at least, the defendant Stoel Loomis received no part of the same.

The dwelling house was continuously occupied by the same tenant until the time of the trial, and the rent fqr it was collected either by Jay Loomis or Rachael Loomis; at least, the defendant Stoel Loomis received no part of the same.

In the case at bar the defendant Stoel W. Loomis should be charged only with the rental value of the property occupied by him from and after the date when he, if at all, commenced to occupy the same in hostility to his co-tenants. He should be charged only with rental for such part as he occupied, and not for the entire premises, as found by the referee. Equitably, the other co-tenants should be charged with the rental of any part of the premises which they occupied in like manner; and it was entirely proper that an accounting between the parties should be had in this action, settling their respective interests to the property in question.

notes: Relevant because the court treated the continued rental of a dwelling house as an ordinary source of rent requiring accounting among cotenants; the identity and status of the person who originally let it are unclear.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division, Fourth Department
holding_summary: A covenant protecting light was appurtenant to the adjoining land and remained enforceable despite the neighborhood's change to business uses. The court emphasized that the former residence, though incorporated into a hotel, remained the O'Connor family's home.

quotes.text: The new building and the old Wile residence are connected and used as a hotel, but the O’Connor family still make their home there.

While the Wile residence has become a part of the hotel, it is still used as a place of. residence by the O’Connor family, and as regards the windows which the covenant; was intended to protect, they are precisely in the same place and condition, and light is just as essential now as when the covenant was made.

We are, however, of the opinion that it was intended by the covenants in the deed from Wile to Butts to burden the nine-foot strip and the three-foot strip with the respective covenants relating thereto, making them servitudes or easements for the benefit of the adjoining lands and becoming appurtenant thereto, and that the rights and burdens thus created followed the respective parcels through the various changes and transmissions- of title.

If the conclusions we have reached are correct, it follows that the plaintiffs are entitled to the relief demanded, since it clearly appears that the construction of this building by the defendant will obstruct the windows and light to the Wile building.

notes: Relevant because the court expressly treated hotel use and continued family residence as compatible, although it did not discuss guest terms, compensation, or room-letting practices.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term, Second Department
holding_summary: The written fixed-term lease of a one-family cottage extended through midnight on May 1, so the tenant who vacated before midnight did not hold over. The judgment imposing rent for May was reversed.

quotes.text: The agreement between the parties is in writing and was entered into on the 18th day of September, 1909. The plaintiff agreed to let, and the defendant agreed to take, a one-family cottage for a term expressed as follows:
“For a term of seven months, to commence on the first day of October, 1909, and to end on the first day of May, 1910.”

A reasonable construction of the terms of the lease and of the agreement continuing it requires the court to hold that under the provisions of both writings the term of the tenant was to end, as a matter of explicit arrangement, on the 1st day of May, 191E This, of course, extended his tenancy until midnight of that day, and under the conceded facts he had vacated the premises within that time.
Judgment reversed, and new trial ordered, with costs to abide event.

notes: Directly relevant as judicial recognition and construction of a compensated, seven-month letting of a one-family dwelling; the record does not show whether the cottage was part of the owner's household or a rental business.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: The landlord was not liable in tort for a residential tenant's fall from an unrailed roof because the condition was open and obvious and did not constitute a nuisance. A promise to add a railing could support contract damages, but not recovery in tort for the personal injuries.

quotes.text: Tíie plaintiff was a tenant of the first floor above'the store in premises owned by the defendant.

The lessor of buildings, in the absence of fraud, or any agreement to that effect, is not liable to tenants, or others lawfully upon the premises by his authority, for their condition, or that they are tenantable, and may be safely" and conveniently used for the purposes for which they were apparently intended.

If this was a defect, it was open and obvious, and known to the tenant. Therefore, if this roof, as a place for hanging clothes, was an appurtenance to the demised premises, no duty rested upon the landlord to alter its construction.

The most that can be claimed for this promise is that the landlord had agreed to put a certain improvement upon the premises to obviate a dangerous condition, and for a breach of that agreement he was liable on the contract, and not in tort.

notes: Marginally relevant because it states substantive rules governing a compensated residential tenancy, but it does not concern short-term occupancy, lodger status, or regulation of letting.
